-The degree of overlap between opto-tagged FS neuron data in Fig 6 and FS neuron data classified by spike width in Fig 4 should be presented in the supplementary figure. If discrepancies exist, these should be discussed.
-In Fig 7B, the authors claim that environmental enrichment (ENR) accelerates learning in the Term group compared to the standardly housed (STD) condition. However, the initial performance on Day 0 appears worse, and there seems to be no difference in final performance or days to reach criterion.
-Since both male and female data were collected, the authors should explicitly show whether there were any sex differences in the supplementary figures.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
POINT-BY-POINT RESPONSE TO REVIEWS
Introduction and response to general concerns
We greatly appreciate the Reviewers’ support, critiques and suggestions, and we think they
significantly improved the manuscript and the quality of our analyses. Before we address the
concerns point by point below, we would like to highlight major revisions to our study. Major
textual revisions are highlighted in light grey throughout the revised manuscript.
1. We consulted Dr. Xin Cynthia Tong, a mathematician in our Department, who is an
expert in quantitative approaches. She helped reanalyze all our data, which we hope
addressed concerns about data analysis. New analysis approaches made some of the
differences between experimental groups even more pronounced, especially in the cue-
evoked firing and the distribution of selectivity indices. While our findings remain the
same, i.e. the representation and processing of task cues in preterm mice is altered
compared to term mice, some of our conclusions are revised considering the new
analyses.
2. Revised analysis revealed that the N of units significantly responsive to the non-
rewarded cue when split by behavioral outcomes for optotagging experiments was too
low to comfortably draw conclusions. We therefore focused the results derived from
optotagged neurons solely on general cue representation, and we moved that data to
the supplementary material. Of note is that the data for fast-spiking neurons isolated
through bulk electrophysiology and the data for optogenetically identified fast-spiking
neurons overlaps to a large degree (new Figure 4 and Supplementary Figures 9 and 10).
3. We separated the data for the visual cortex neurons into regular and fast-spiking
neurons and to our surprise found that both neuronal populations exhibit similar task-
related hyperactivity. We revised our discussion to incorporate these new findings,
especially since the prefrontal cortex shows a different pattern of activity in RS and FS
neurons during the task.
4. To give more credence to our previous suggestion that preterm PFC resembles
adolescent PFC, we trained adolescent term mice in our task, recorded their prefrontal
activity and compared the cue representation to that of preterm mice (new Figure 6 and
Supplementary Figure 11). While our results haven’t fully recapitulated the Nieves and
Liston preprint we cite in the original submission (likely due to methodology differences),
we did find remarkable similarities between adolescents and adult term mice in the
representation and processing of the non-rewarded cue. We discuss these in the revised
manuscript, and we think that the adolescent data will be a valuable resource to the field.
5. In the original manuscript, we use the term “Modulation Index” to determine the degree
of responsivity of neurons to task cues. We revised this term to “Selectivity Index” as our
literature search found that Modulation Index is typically used to denote firing rate
alterations by behavioral states, such as attention. To emphasize that we measure
responsiveness to the sensory cues, we chose to use Selectivity Index instead. While
this was not an issue brought up by the reviewers, it was brought up by the
neuroscience community as the submission was accessible as a preprint.
Point-by-point responses are below with the Reviewer comments italicized.

increased firing to go-cue but reduced modulation in ACC to the no-go cue. These results are
compared to other data showing similar results in adolescent mice to suggest pre-term mice
maintain a persistent ‘adolescent’ mode of processing that is impairing their task performance.
This is an important set of physiological findings that leads to an interesting conceptual
conclusion. This work is an important advance in our understanding of the circuit and cognitive
basis of neural issues linked to preterm birth. Overall the manuscript is very well written, the
studies are properly designed, appropriately powered (within the limitations of mouse ephys),
and appropriately analyzed.
I do believe there is one major sticking point that needs to be addressed before this work can be
published, as well as a number of major improvements that should be considered to increase
the impact of the work.
Critical point: Firing rates for ostensible single units throughout the study are nearly an order of
magnitude higher than other published studies. The resting rates are similar to visually evoked
rates observed by multiple other labs. This undermines confidence in the results, which are
likely multi-units or severely biased to very high firing rate sub-populations. This discrepancy
needs to resolved and integrated into the interpretation of the results.
We thank the reviewer for bringing this up, as well as for their later comments which
helped us resolve this discrepancy. In the original submission, we present our firing rate data
throughout the manuscript as mean±SEM. However, and as the reviewer pointed out, the firing
rate distribution is log-normal and largely reported as median±IQ range/MAD. For example in
the V1, Durand et al. report these values: L2/3 0.58 ± 0.11, L4 3.00 ± 1.14, and L5 2.86 ± 0.65
sp/s, with an average of 1.88 ± 0.25 for spontaneous, outside of any task context, activity in the
awake V1 of adult mice (Durand et al., 2016). These values are for units unsorted by width into
fast and regular spiking (FS and RS). Please note that they did not report whether the spread of
data reported is IQR or another measure. We separated our data into Upper (putative 2/3) and
Lower (4-6) layers through analysis of visually evoked potentials (VEPs), where layer 4 has the
shortest latency VEP. and found somewhat higher values in adult term mice: Upper layers:

but we found the same to be true for the PFC.

is never perfect, and we discuss this in the revised manuscript. However, Durand et al. also
reported that mice rarely ran or walked during the recordings, which is why they did not
separate the data into stationary and moving. In our hands, habituated adult mice typically
spend a significant amount of time on the treadmill walking at different speeds, which is why we

somewhat elevated the firing rates in our dataset as locomotion is known to enhance them (Niell

Major points:
(1) Unless I am mistaken, the correlation of preterm behavior and ephys with ‘adolescent’
coding is based on a single pre-print, which used calcium imaging to an auditory cue. While the
similarities are indeed pretty striking, the absence of relevant adolescent data in this paper and

The reviewer is correct-the study we cite remains a preprint, and it used a different
methodology. We, however, decided to pursue this issue experimentally as we were
unsuccessful in our attempts to identify the circuit(s) that drive the impairments in preterm mice
(please see our response to Reviewer 3). We were able to confirm some similarities between
adolescent and adult preterm PFC: they both have a weak representation of the non-rewarded
cue in RS neurons, the peristimulus time histograms (PSTHs) of their prefrontal FS neurons
during the task are very similar, and their evoked responses to the non-rewarded cue classify
the behavioral outcomes to that cue at a similar accuracy (Figures 6 and Supplementary Figure

title was not justified and we have replaced it with what we think is the main finding of our study,
as the reviewer suggested.
Some of our findings are different from the Nieves and Liston, 2023, but we think that is due to
methodology used. As the reviewer mentioned, Nieves and Liston used 2-photon imaging after
an auditory task, while we used electrophysiology in a visual task. These two approaches, while
complementary, detect different cell populations. Despite this, we were able to confirm their

(2) There is no discussion of the potential depth of the units recorded. It is not required they

located is important.
This is an important point-we now state that the neurons in the V1 are recorded from all layers.
For the PFC, most of our recordings were from deeper portion of layer 2/3 going to layer 6 as
we tried to avoid recording close to the midline (see minor points response). We revised Figure
4 to include an image of the electrode tracks.
(3) Percentage of visually responsive units in V1 and firing rate increases to preferred
orientation should be presented.
The percentage of units that are considered selective for oriented gratings is presented in
Figure 1d and this is what we define as visually-responsive for this study. We clarify this now in
the methods section in the revised manuscript (lines 218-220), and we also report the firing rate
increase to the preferred orientation (over baseline, line 309-312). We find that our values are
similar to what other studies report [such as (Wang et al., 2010), which also reports the fraction
of neurons with OSI>0.3].
(4) Why no separation of FS and RS neurons in V1 as for AAC? If there is no compelling reason
these should be separated and analyzed as for AAC.
We include the separation of V1 neurons into FS and RS in the revised manuscript (new Figure
3) and we would like to thank the reviewers for bringing this up-indeed, there was no reason to
omit it in the first place, and we apologize for this lapse. We found that both RS and FS neurons
in preterm V1 have elevated firing during the task. While surprising, as we expected weakened
inhibition like in the PFC, this is in line with the powerful top-down modulation of the V1 during
task performance.
(5) Why does the analysis switch to z-score normalized firing rates in figure 5? For comparison
with previous data absolute firing rates should be used, unless there is a compelling reason.
We present all data now as raw firing rates. While PSTHs are the only instance where the firing
rates are presented as mean±SEM, we changed the scale to logarithmic to indicate that the
data is not normally distributed.
(6) lines 241-242 Firing rates are rarely normally distributed, but more likely to be log-normal.
Normal descriptive statistics (mean/SEM) are likely inappropriate so should use log transformed
or non-normal appropriate (median, percentiles).
As suggested, we changed all our reporting of log-normally distributed data to median±MAD
and indicate in the Methods that all data was first tested for normality before conducting other
analyses.
Minor
Were all animals recorded included in the analysis, or were some excluded for technical
reasons?
We now clarify which animals were excluded from the study and from analysis in the methods
section (line 184-190). Animals were excluded from study for health reasons, while animals that
were excluded from analysis either did not have the electrode in the correct location or the
location was unconfirmed, or they had large motion or blood vessel pulsation artifacts. Artifacts
were present more often in animals that took longer to reach the criterion or in animals where
the craniotomy over the PFC was very close to the midline because of the sinus.

This was a copy/paste error and we apologize-6 orientations, which we corrected in the revised
version.

Yes, but we removed that term from the revised version of the manuscript.

of the conclusions, before pursuing with the review.
We appreciate the concerns brought up and we have completely revised our analysis for the
resubmission. We consulted with a colleague who is a mathematician and an expert statistician
(Dr. Xin Cynthia Tong), who helped us reanalyze all the data. We would like to add that she
brought up the same concerns after reading the first version of the manuscript. While our main
findings after reanalysis did not change, some of the conclusions did, as the reviewer (correctly)
implied.
Lines 192-193: what do the authors mean with “Unit waveforms were further compared between
optotagging and task recordings for quality assurance.”?
We added a line immediately after that sentence (line 226-228) to clarify that a change in unit
amplitude of 10% or more between the two recording sessions warranted the exclusion of that
unit from analyses as such high amplitude variability indicates either unit/probe drift or multiunit
contamination.
Lines 194-200: this paragraph is quite unclear. The authors refer to a Rvar, but this variable
does not appear in the formula that is given. Also: paired t-test seems like an inappropriate test
for a log-distributed variable like firing rate. Lastly, what is the rationale of double-dipping with a
t-test first and then then a comparison of z-scored AUCs?
Rvar was a copy/paste error and we apologize. This is corrected in the revised version of the
manuscript. In the revised version, we reanalyzed our unit data with tests appropriate for log-
normally distributed data. For determining significant cue modulation, Wilcoxon paired signed
rank test was used, for comparison of firing rates Mann Whitney test was used, and we used K-
S test to compare distributions (all of these and others are indicated in the methods and
appropriate sections throughout the manuscript). Instead of t-tests of AUCs, we use the
permutation test of PSTH AUCs in the revised version of the manuscript. While our results
remained largely the same, the significance is different with the new analysis.
Lines 232-233: could the authors speculate as to what a day of prematurity in mice corresponds
in human pregnancies?
We briefly discuss this in the revised manuscript (line 865-872), but we must admit that this
comparison remains a challenge and a contentious issue in the field. Most studies consider
mice during the first week to 10 days of life an equivalent of a third trimester fetus, some of
which is based on electrophysiological comparison of rodent and human developing cortices
(Colonnese et al., 2010). Our unpublished data indicates that in terms of electrophysiological
activity, mice and humans share a similar developmental trajectory from birth through the first 2
weeks and one year of life, respectively, and that birth itself plays a role in patterning the
perinatal intrinsic activity in mice (which is the line of research that led us to test the long term
consequences of advancing the birth timing). Current models of prematurity-related brain injury
(term mice subjected to hypoxia and/or ischemia) do not capture the actual prematurity that, at
least according to our findings, itself has an impact on brain development. It will be important to
compare the prefrontal function in term mice subjected to hypoxia/ischemia to those in the
current study and relate both to findings in humans.
Lines 241-243: I do not think that it is appropriate to test differences in firing rates with a t-test. I
suggest to log-transform the data if the authors want to use a test that assumes normality.
Further, what is a nested t-test? By looking at GraphPad guides, it seems that the test that is
used is a linear mixed-effect model, but I am not sure that this is the case. If it is indeed the
case, I suggest that the authors use this terminology, which is much more common than “nested
t-test”. This part should also be better explained in the Methods section.
The reviewer is right, and we corrected this-we now use Wilcoxon signed rank test for pre-post
comparisons and Mann-Whitney or K-S test for comparison between groups. We reanalyzed all
the data for the revised version of the manuscript and removed the nested tests, which should
make the terminology clearer, along with the analysis itself.
Lines 244-248: to what do the degrees of freedom refer to? Did the authors use a nested
statistical test also in this analysis?
We revised this analysis completely, and we compare values obtained per mouse-we explained
this with more detail in the revised version.
Lines 262-3: do any of the provided references show that there is a monosynaptic connection
from V1 to the ACC?
Thank you for pointing this out-we added (Zhang et al., 2016) which shows exactly that.
Lines 264-281: I have many doubts about the statistical analysis:
- Are the authors running two separate models to compare Term vs MFP Term and Term vs
MFP Term vs Preterm? If so, I do not understand the rational for this. I would suggest to only
run one model with the three groups, which should also simplify the manner in which statistical
results are reported.
We have done this for the revised manuscript.
- Why is there only one pvalue when comparing Term, MPF Term and Preterm? Are the authors
aggregating the first two groups?
Yes, as originally both term groups were aggregated into a single one as there were no
statistical differences between them. In the revised manuscript we separated them and report all
group comparisons.
- Why are the authors reporting R2 when the variable of interest is the slope?
We removed the linear regression from the trajectory analyses and rely solely on linear mixed-
models in the revised manuscript, which described our data better.
- Are the numbers used to run the Chi2 test 0/22, 0/19 and 5/29? If so, how can these values
lead to the reported p-value? If not, could the authors give the exact values that were used?
We replaced Chi-square for most analyses with K-S test in the revised version as it can handle
zero values. All data is provided in source data file.
Lines 308-311: in previous instances in which data was nested (see lines 241-243), the authors
seemingly took this into account when comparing means, but this does not seem to be the case
for this analysis. I suggest that the authors re-run the analysis while keeping in consideration the
nestedness of their data.
PSTHs of neurons are typically compared with Ns of units in literature, and we did not want to
deviate from that. However, we replaced the means comparison with permutation test of the
AUCs.
Lines 308-316: why does the number of units change between the two analyses?
The number of neurons significantly modulated by the cue is different between the two cues, as
well as between the behavioral outcomes to the cues. For the comparison of PSTHs and
selectivity indices (SIs), we considered only significantly modulated neurons. We clarify this in
the methods section of the revised manuscript and report it as % of all neurons in the results to
make this point clear.
Lines 312-316: if the increase in firing rate is context-specific, why is it elevated also before the
stimulus is administered?
We corrected this to “task-specific”. The firing rates in preterm mice are elevated as soon as
they are placed in the context of the task, which is why they are elevated before the cues as
well. We clarified this point in the revised version of the manuscript.
Figures 3D-3H: why are the authors binning the MI and then modeling their data with a Chi2
test? I don’t understand the rational for binning. This data would be much more straightforwardly
analyzed without binning and with a simple linear-mixed effect model. If the authors even want
to consider that the variable can only vary between -1 and 1, they could use a generalized linear
mixed-effect model, but this might be an overkill judging by the distribution of the Mis (rather
towards 0 than the extrema). If you use a Chi2, you are not testing for differences in means
anymore.
This is an important point which we clarified in the revised version-we are comparing the
distributions of the indices and not their means/medians, as the populations can have very
similar means through different distributions. We think that distribution is more important for
selectivity index. We also renamed the modulation index to selectivity index as our literature
search found that modulation is used more for state-dependent processes, and selectivity for
the sensory cues.
Figure 3E and lines 338-339: as in lines 264-281, I do not understand how such a small % of
inhibited neurons can lead to the reported p-values. What data went into this test? Since the
effect has to be tested on a mouse level, I also suggest to improve the visualization of the data
to understand the consistency of the effect on an individual mouse level (e.g. plot the %
of neurons that are activated/inhibited/not affected in individual mice).
We tested this on a mouse level in the revised version of the manuscript and came to different
conclusions (new Figure 3 and Supplementary Figure 5). While we tried to include all points in
these graphs, it was a challenge to make them readable, which is why we added the Reward/No
Reward preference graphs that represent the distribution of the mouse data.
Lines 374-375: still linear mixed-effect model? Please provide details
This analysis was revised in the new version of the manuscript, where we analyzed the data per
animal (lines 495-497).
Lines 376-378: why ignore nestedness when this was not the case when comparing firing rates
in prior parts (see comments above) of the manuscript?
This was revised in the new version of the manuscript, which now represents per mouse data
(line 498).
Lines 379-383: what are the values that went into this Chi2?
Figures 4F-G-H-I, see previous comments on Chi2 on continuous data and Figure 3E.
Figures 5C-D-F-G, see previous comments on Chi2 on continuous data and Figure 3E.
Figures 6E-G-H-I, see previous comments on Chi2 on continuous data and Figure 3E.
All these analyses were revised in the new version of the manuscript (Chi-square is no longer
used for this type of data).
Line 986: there is a typo. It should be “white”, not “while”.
We corrected this.
Reviewer #3
In this study, the authors investigate how preterm birth affects cognitive function and visual
information processing by recording neural activity in the V1 and ACC of mice during a Go/No-
go task using electrophysiological techniques. They demonstrate that preterm mice exhibit a
higher FA rate in the Go/No-go task, despite showing comparable orientation selectivity in V1
neurons to term controls. Furthermore, they show that both V1 and ACC neurons in preterm
mice respond differently to visual stimuli during the task. Using optogenetic tagging, they also
identify abnormalities in the visual processing of V1-projecting ACC neurons and ACC-FS
neurons. The authors conducted experiments using both male and female mice, employed
appropriate control groups, and used suitable methods and analyses to address the important
question of how preterm birth impacts cognitive function. However, as described more in detail
below, there are significant limitations to the interpretation of the data. Notably, the study lacks
an investigation of causality, which diminishes its impact.
Major comments:
1) The study does not provide any causal link between neural activity changes of studied circuit
(V1 projecting ACC neurons or FS-ACC neurons) and behavioral changes (increased FA) in
pre-term mice. A key hypothesis in this manuscript is that overactivation of ACC-FS neurons
leads to decreased activity of V1-projecting ACC neurons, resulting in reduced V1 activity in No-
go trial and an increased FA rate. However, none of these causal relationships have been
demonstrated, leaving the study less mechanistic. Without a demonstration of direct
manipulations of neural circuits during behavior impacting behavior, observed neural changes
may not be related to behavioral changes, leaving the study descriptive.
We agree with the reviewer and emphasize in the revised version that our study is descriptive,
and we discuss this limitation. We have attempted to test for causality in both ACC→V1 circuit
and in FS neurons with no success, some of which was due to methodological limitations, as we
outline below.
Firstly, we tried to manipulate both ACC→V1 and prefrontal FS neurons optogenetically but
found that prolonged light stimulation (2x day for 50 x 3 s duration) at levels that had a
physiological impact on neuronal firing led to neurotoxicity. Reducing the cue duration to 2
instead of 3 seconds did not mitigate this. We next attempted to suppress the activity of
ACC→V1 circuit with chemogenetics, which unexpectedly elevated V1 firing in controls (term
mice, see Figure 2a). Increasing the activity of FS neurons through chemogenetics in adult
preterm mice failed to improve their behavior in a pilot experiment (Figure 2b). We did not
include this data in the manuscript as the data from ACC→V1 activation will be a part on
another manuscript, and the pilot experiment with chemogenetic activation of interneurons did
not warrant collecting a full dataset. Further, after collecting the adolescent data (new Figure 6),
we now think that there is a developmental window during which these manipulations might
have more of an effect. We also mention this in our response to Reviewer 2, but our preliminary
data indicates that the alterations in the firing of prefrontal neurons in preterm mice begin at
birth, further indicating that there is a defined window for interventions after preterm birth. We
are actively addressing this issue in another study as it is beyond the scope of this manuscript.
To increase the significance of our findings and to try to shed more light on the developmental
impact of preterm birth on the PFC, we added data describing cue processing in adolescent
mice and compared it to preterm mice. We found several similarities in the representation of the
non-rewarded cue and the activity of FS neurons, which we discuss in details in the revised
version (Figure 6, Supplementary Figure 11 and associated Results and Discussion sections).
Figure 2. a) PSTH of V1 firing after administration of CNO (2.5 mg/kg) and vehicle (DMSO) to mice 30 minutes
before the onset of training. Mice were transduced with inhibitory DREADD G1 in V1-projecting PFC neurons.
Significant firing rate increase is present with CNO administration. b) Comparison of behavioral performance
of preterm mice from Figure 2 of the manuscript and preterm mice injected with S5E2-Gq in the PFC (Gq in
fast-spiking interneurons) and treated with CNO (2.5 mg/kg) 30 minutes before each training session. While
this preliminary cohort includes only 5 mice, the overlap with the standard preterm group indicates no effect of
fast-spiking interneuron activation on behavior in preterm mice.
2) It is unclear if the observed neural and behavioral deficits in preterm mice reflect deficits in
learning or/and discrimination. Throughout the manuscript, these two concepts are not clearly
considered separately. Due to the trajectory difference (especially FA) during training phase, it is
highly likely that there is a deficit in learning. Demonstration of neural correlate of learning
trajectory would be informative to enhance the mechanistic significance of this study (especially
if the study does not provide causal link between circuit activity and behavior).
This is an important point-the deficit in preterm mice is a learning deficit and we clarify this in the
revised version. In the original version, we used the terms interchangeably which is incorrect
and as the reviewer pointed out, preterm mice have a learning deficit (and not discrimination).
We now added new data that indicates altered encoding of behavioral outcomes to the non-
rewarded cue in preterm and adolescent mice, as well as a finding that re responses to the
rewarded cue are predictive of performance in preterm but not term mice, further providing
support for divergent mechanisms of learning in the two groups of mice (new Figures 4, 5 and
6). We discuss these, especially in the context of behavioral inhibition.
3) Given that V1 activity is known to be enhanced by locomotion, extent and timing of
locomotion on the treadmill during the task should be analyzed to rule out that neural changes
are not confounded by locomotion.
We discuss this also in our response to Reviewer 1, where there is an example of motion during
a recording session. We added motion tracking data during behavioral sessions to the revised
manuscript (Supplementary Figure 4A of the revised manuscript). We found no significant
differences in the extent or the timing of motion between term and preterm mice during task
performance, indicating that the elevated firing rates in preterm mice have a different origin.
4) Preterm mice show a lower Hit rate even in the naïve state (Fig 2G). This raises questions
about potential motivational deficits, which can be assessed by different tasks such as
progressive ratio test.
While we were unable to add the progressive ratio test, we analyzed the lick frequencies during
the training session as a proxy for motivation (Berditchevskaia et al., 2016). We indeed found
that lick rates significantly drop during the session, but all animal groups had a similar reduction
in lick frequencies, indicating that the motivation of preterm mice during the task is comparable
to term mice. The reviewer correctly points out low lick rates in naïve preterm mice, but they
increase throughout the training and surpass those of term mice (Supplementary Figure 4C of
the revised manuscript). We, however, plan to pursue tasks that can address motivation as well
as attention better than the current one in our future studies.
5) While the activity of FS and RS neurons is analyzed separately in Fig 4, the activity of V1
neurons in Fig 3 is not divided into these categories. It is unclear why FS and RS neurons were
not differentiated for V1 activity, particularly as the distinction between excitatory and inhibitory
neurons in V1 could provide critical insights into the observed changes.
We agree and we have added this to the revised manuscript (new Figure 3). Indeed, our data
further indicates the involvement of top-down areas in observed V1 firing changes in preterm
mice, especially since both RS and FS neurons are equally affected.
6) Inclusion of “Adolescent-like” in the title misleading. While author cited relevant literatures,
they did not examine the neural activity nor behavior using the same task used in this study.
Authors should consider conducting experiments in adolescent mice to support the claim, or
“Adolescent-like” should be removed from the title, result section, and limited to the discussion
section.
This is a very important point. As the reviewer pointed out, the connections we made with
adolescent processing were based on a different study and purely speculative. For the revision,
we trained adolescent term mice in our task and recorded their prefrontal activity (new Figure 6).
We indeed found similarities in the representation and processing of the non-rewarded cue in
adolescent and preterm mice. Still, and as we mention in our response to Reviewer 1, the
differences in the processing of the rewarded cue warrant removal of “adolescent-like” from the
title and the manuscript text. Instead, we focused on describing the differences and similarities
between the two groups of mice, as well as on larger implications of our findings. We were able
to confirm some of the findings from Nieves and Liston, 2023 and we think that the adolescent
data will be a valuable addition to the field. The differences we found in our task between term
adolescent and adult mice in prefrontal activity warrant their own study, which we are currently
pursuing.
Other comments:
-In Fig 2C, the Miss marker (water droplet) is present, but the cross marker is missing.
We corrected this in the revised version (minus is added instead of a cross).
-How were trained mice defined in Fig 2G? Were only animals that passed the criteria included,
or were all animals analyzed at their final session? If the latter, it would be important to compare
only those that passed the criteria to see whether FA rate differences remain.
Thank you for bringing this up-we now clarify in detail that-all term born mice passed the
criterion within the 4000 trial limit (lines 175-176 and 325-327). For preterm mice, all mice were
included and analyzed at the last session, which for mice that did not pass the criterion is the
session on the 20th day of training. As the reviewer suggested, we compared the mice that
passed the criteria and the FA differences remained, albeit the p value was higher (line 353-
362). We also must note that all our electrophysiological data is from mice with similar d’ values,
demonstrating divergent processing of task cues and in term and preterm mice. We included
this in the revised version of the manuscript (line 597-601).
-In Fig 3G, V1 activity during FA trials does not appear to increase significantly in the Term
group. The sustained activity in V1 shown in Fig 3C should be further discussed regarding
whether it genuinely reflects premotor activity.
This is an important point-we removed this wording from the manuscript for 2 reasons: 1) the
space limitations did not accommodate a full discussion in this manuscript, and 2) a detailed
study of task-related sustained activity in the V1 is ongoing in our laboratory and a part of
another manuscript in which we are addressing the role of this activity in behavior. It is important
to note that licks to the rewarded cue occur in bouts (Figure 3), whereas for False Alarm trials
they typically happen as a few licks with random timing, so any increases in activity related to
licking are lost by averaging. Still, the current data in this manuscript is not sufficient to imply
that sustained activity reflects premotor activity, which is why we removed it from the
manuscript.
Figure 3. Example of licks and behavioral outcomes, with visible lick bouts of many licks to the rewarded cue
(Hits/H) and few licks to the non-rewarded cue during False Alarms (FA). CR: Correct Rejection.
-The authors claim that elevated firing rates in preterm mice are unlikely due to licking during
the task (L312), but Supplementary Fig S3 shows that Preterm mice have significantly more
licks per trial than Term mice. Without investigating the correlation between lick count and
sustained activity, this conclusion is premature. Correlating lick count with sustained activity and
demonstrating a lack of correlation would strengthen this argument.
We performed this analysis for the revised manuscript and found no correlation between
sustained activity and lick frequency (Supplementary Figure 4D). In preterm mice, the
relationship between the two appeared inverse even, which would not be the case if sustained
activity reflected lick related activity. We also computed correlograms for both V1 and PFC
where we show peaks in their activity occur significantly prior to onset of licks (new Figures 3D
and 4C).
-Fig 3D shows a distribution of MI values where some V1 neurons exhibit higher MI and others
lower MI in Preterm mice. It is unclear whether the average MI for V1 neurons in Preterm mice
is genuinely higher than for neurons in Term mice. Showing vertical lines indicating group
means would clarify this point.
We changed the plots to make the distributions more visible and now clearly indicate median
values. Means are indeed similar for several SI groups from term and preterm mice, but we are
comparing the distribution of indices in our study which we think is more informative, especially
as means can overlap in two different distributions (Reviewer 2 brought up a similar concern).
For example, a higher number of positively modulated neurons with high SI values will give a tail
to the distribution, but the difference in means may be marginal if the rest of the population is
equally distributed compared to the other group. However, high SI values indicate that these
neurons receive strong sensory or cue-related inputs, and the opposite is true for low SI values.
This is evident in revised Figure 4H, where a negative tail is present in the SI values for the non-
rewarded cue in preterm mice, indicating that a fraction of their prefrontal neurons is suppressed
after the non-rewarded cue, which is not the case in term mice.
-Are the data in Fig 4E limited to RS neurons? Clearly separating RS and FS neurons and
presenting the data would improve clarity.
We revised this figure and now both RS and FS are included.
-Figure 4K is missing.
This was corrected.
-The statement on L427 ("stronger positive modulation by the rewarded cue despite no change
in the firing rates") is confusing. Since MI is calculated using firing rates, the claim of "no change
in firing rates" is misleading. While statistical significance may not have been detected,
differences are evident in the traces.
This statement was removed, and we revised this and similar descriptions to simpler and more
accurate sentences.
-The claim in L443 that deficits are "not as severe as in the V1" (Fig 3) is unclear. Based on the
MI values, changes in V1-projecting ACC neurons appear larger. Moreover, throughout the
manuscript, the overlap between the bars of MI histograms for each group makes it difficult to
interpret the data. Adjusting the colors or the presentation style of the graphs could improve
readability.
We swapped the histograms for raincloud plots which made the distributions more visible and
added a line for medians. As mentioned, we moved the optotagging data to Supplementary
Material. We appreciate this feedback these data are key for some of the conclusions and it is
vital that the figures are readable.
-The degree of overlap between opto-tagged FS neuron data in Fig 6 and FS neuron data
classified by spike width in Fig 4 should be presented in the supplementary figure. If
discrepancies exist, these should be discussed.
We now included the FS data to Figure 4 and moved the optotagged data to Supplementary as
our revised statistical approaches indicated an insufficient N for some analyses. The data is
largely overlapping, with discrepancies in the firing rates as originally reported, likely due to
more low-firing neurons being detected with optotagging.
-In Fig 7B, the authors claim that environmental enrichment (ENR) accelerates learning in the
Term group compared to the standardly housed (STD) condition. However, the initial
performance on Day 0 appears worse, and there seems to be no difference in final performance
or days to reach criterion.
We revised the statistical analysis for this dataset, as well as our conclusions. The reviewer
correctly identified that the performance in term group was slightly worse than in standardly-
reared term mice, which our previous statistical tests failed to pick up on. We used linear mixed
models for comparison of all learning trajectories in the revised manuscript and identified other
potential effects of birth, as well as of sex (see point below). We discuss the potential reasons
for the negative effect of ENR in the revised version (lines 830-835).
-Since both male and female data were collected, the authors should explicitly show whether
there were any sex differences in the supplementary figures.
Supplementary Figure 2 now shows sex-segregated data and we report the effects of sex in
lines (lines 353-362). To our surprise, we found that females overall have lower d’ values in our
task, but we also found that birth impacts both sexes to a comparable degree. While it is
currently unclear why females of all groups perform worse in our task, we plan to address this in
our future studies.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
The authors addressed the majority of reviewers’ concerns (statistical analysis methods, clarifying that the study is descriptive, adding new adolescent data, motion tracking, lick rate, etc, included the distinction between learning and discrimination and discussed their methodological limitations). However, the following is insufficient.
In response to Reviewer 3's Key Comment 1, the authors state:
"Furthermore, after collecting adolescent data (new Figure 6), we believe there may be a developmental window during which these manipulations may be more effective. We also mentioned this point in our response to Reviewer 2, but preliminary data indicate that changes in the firing of prefrontal cortex neurons in preterm mice begin at birth, suggesting a clear window for intervention after preterm birth. This issue is beyond the scope of this manuscript and is being actively addressed in a separate study."
This statement is unclear. They propose experiments based on data that has not been shown. Additional data or a detailed explanation is required. Furthermore, any related statements cannot be found in their responses to Reviewer 2 (and Reviewer 1).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_6: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
POINT-BY-POINT RESPONSE TO REVIEWS
Reviewers #5 and #6 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors addressed the majority of reviewers’ concerns (statistical analysis methods,
clarifying that the study is descriptive, adding new adolescent data, motion tracking, lick rate,
etc, included the distinction between learning and discrimination and discussed their
methodological limitations). However, the following is insufficient.
In response to Reviewer 3's Key Comment 1, the authors state:
"Furthermore, after collecting adolescent data (new Figure 6), we believe there may be a
developmental window during which these manipulations may be more effective. We also
mentioned this point in our response to Reviewer 2, but preliminary data indicate that changes
in the firing of prefrontal cortex neurons in preterm mice begin at birth, suggesting a clear
window for intervention after preterm birth. This issue is beyond the scope of this manuscript
and is being actively addressed in a separate study."
This statement is unclear. They propose experiments based on data that has not been shown.
Additional data or a detailed explanation is required. Furthermore, any related statements
cannot be found in their responses to Reviewer 2 (and Reviewer 1).
Our response
Firstly, we would like to thank the Reviewers for taking the time to review the manuscript as well
as our response to the previous round of reviews. In the revised version of the manuscript, we
now discuss the developmental mechanism that may be impaired in preterm mice from birth.
While we do not provide additional data from our laboratory, we cite studies with strong
evidence supporting our reasoning.
Briefly, previous studies indicate that preterm mice have reduced extracellular (CSF) serotonin
concentrations during the first few days after birth (Toda et al., 2013). Given the vital roles of
perinatal serotonin signaling the development of prefrontal neurons, and in the maturation of
adult behaviors (new references 98-109 in the revised manuscript), we hypothesize that
reduced serotonin concentrations in neonate preterm mice negatively impact the development
and/or maturation of circuits that guide reward-driven behaviors in adult mice. We discuss this in
the revised version of the manuscript, lines 857-865. While experiments that will test this
hypothesis are beyond the scope of this study, our laboratory is actively working on them
(R01MH140184).

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Preterm birth is a leading risk factor for atypicalities in cognitive and sensory processing, but it is unclear how prematurity impacts circuits that support these functions. To address this, we trained adult male and female mice born a day early (preterm mice) on a visual discrimination task and found that they fail to achieve high levels of performance due to increased responding to the non-rewarded cue. The representation of the non-rewarded cue in the prefrontal cortex (PFC), a brain area that mediates response inhibition, is significantly weaker in regular spiking, putative pyramidal neurons in preterm mice, while their fast-spiking interneurons show blunted responses to both task cues. Similar cue representation is present in the PFC of adolescent term-born mice, suggesting that preterm birth disrupts prefrontal maturation. Altogether, our study describes the long-term impact of preterm birth on prefrontal circuits and highlights their sensitivity to traumatic experiences during the perinatal period.

---

## Introduction

Children born prematurely (<37 weeks of gestation) are at 4-5x higher risk for developing intellectual disability (ID) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), at 10x higher risk for developing autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and display persistent deficits in executive function and academic performance. As preterm labor occurs in >10% of all births in the US and worldwide, preterm birth is the leading risk factor for cognitive and neurodevelopmental conditions. Yet, the neural circuits whose function may be disrupted by preterm birth are still unknown.

Impairments in the structure and function of the frontal cortex are frequently associated with executive dysfunction and neurodevelopmental conditions with high incidence in the preterm population. Unsurprisingly, neuroimaging and neurophysiological studies in preterm infants and children revealed reduced volume of and connectivity between frontal, thalamic, and sensory areas. On a cellular level, studies of postmortem prefrontal cortex samples obtained from preterm fetuses demonstrated reduced density of inhibitory interneurons and altered expression of genes related to inhibitory neurotransmission. Some of the changes in brain structure can be recapitulated in animal models of prematurity, which also display disrupted layer-specific distribution and proportion of cortical interneurons, and alterations in the expression of multiple neurotransmission markers. Behaviorally, animal models of prematurity often display persistent hyperactivity, and some cognitive deficits, but the association between preterm birth-related changes in the frontal cortex and high incidence of cognitive dysfunction in the preterm population remains unclear.

To address this, we performed a detailed neurophysiological study of prefrontal function in adult mice born prematurely that were trained on a prefrontal cortex (PFC)-dependent visual discrimination task. While adult mice born 1 day early do not display any changes in baseline visual processing and locomotor activity, they show a significantly impaired learning trajectory. Preterm mice respond more than term mice to the non-rewarded cue, have weaker representation of the non-rewarded cue in the PFC, and show disinhibition of neuronal firing during task performance. Cue representation in regular-spiking (RS) and evoked activity of fast-spiking (FS) neurons in the adult preterm PFC resemble those of adolescent term-born mice, suggesting that preterm birth disrupts prefrontal maturation. Together, our study describes circuit- and cell-type-specific impairments in prefrontal function and top-down sensory processing after preterm birth, paving a path towards uncovering the circuit mechanisms of cognitive dysfunction in the preterm-born population.
