## Methods

Mice
Mice were maintained on C57BL/6 background (The Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME) on reverse 12:12 light:dark cycle (lights off 11 AM-11 PM), with food and water ad libitum, except during visual discrimination training (see below). Animals of both sexes were used between postnatal day 21 and 7 months of age. Preterm mice were generated through timed breedings, where the day after the pairing was considered as gestational day (GD) 0. Once the pregnancy was confirmed (>1.5g increase in weight at GD10), pregnant dams were habituated to handlers by daily handling sessions. Mifepristone (MFP, MiliporeSigma, Burlington, MA or Hello Bio, Bristol, UK) was dissolved in DMSO (MiliporeSigma) and 150µg was injected subcutaneously on GD17. Preterm mice were delivered on GD18. The cage with preterm mice was occasionally supplemented with external heat and oxygen to prevent hypothermia and hypoxia, commonly observed in preterm mice. Control term mice were obtained from timed pregnant dams injected with DMSO on GD17, and with MFP on GD18. All dams received continuous enrichment in form of plastic igloos and nesting material, as well as sunflower seeds (Bio-Serv, Flemington, NJ) beginning 3-4 days before parturition. Animals were treated in accordance with the University of Virginia Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee guidelines.

Environmental enrichment
Nursing dams with their litter were transferred to a standard rat cage when the pups reached postnatal day (P) 5. Dams were co-housed with a nursing dam and its litter that was age matched and on BALB/c strain (purchased from Jackson Laboratory) to facilitate social enrichment. Cages contained multiple enrichment objects: InnoDome and Inno-Wheels from BioServ, gnawing sticks, multiple nesting pads, shredded paper and hay for building nests, as well as a variety of chew toys (pumice chews, willow twigs, willow balls, veggie chews, and hay tunnels, hideaways and sticks). Large enrichment objects were rearranged in the cage every 2 days, while chew toys were replaced with new ones every 2-3 days. Once the litters reached P25, they were weaned and group-housed in standard cages at 2-3 mice/cage to allow for placement of an InnoDome and InnoWheel, as well as 2-3 small chew toys. When the mice reached P60, they were prepared for visual discrimination task as described below.

Viruses
Following viruses were purchased from Addgene: AAV-S5E2-ChR2-mCherry (135634-AAV1; 2×1013 vg/ml), AAV-EF1a-double floxed-hChR2(H134R)-mCherry-WPRE-HGHpA (20297-AAV9; 3.2x1013 vg/ml) and AAV-hSyn-HI-eGFP-Cre-WPRE-SV40 (105540-AAVrg; 1.7x1013 vg/ml). All viruses were diluted 1:10 in sterile PBS before the injection.

Surgeries
Animals were anesthetized with isoflurane in oxygen (2-2.5% induction, 1–1.5% maintenance), warmed with a heating pad at 38°C and given subcutaneous injections of Buprenorphine SR (1mg/kg) or Rimadyl (5mg/kg) and 0.25% Bupivacaine (beneath their scalp). Eyes were covered with Puralube (Decra, Northwich, UK). Scalp and fascia from Bregma to behind lambda were removed, and the skull was cleaned, dried and covered with a thin layer of Scotchbond adhesive (3M, Maplewood, MN). Skin edges were sealed with VetBond (3M).

For virus injections, the head was immobilized in a custom-made stereotactic apparatus and small craniotomies were made on the left hemisphere with a dental drill at the following coordinates: primary visual cortex (V1): 0.5 mm anterior to lambda, 2-3 mm lateral to midline; anterior cingulate cortex (ACC): 2-2.5 mm anterior to bregma, 0.2-0.5 mm lateral to midline. NanoFil syringe (35G beveled needle; WPI, Sarasota, FL) was then used to inject the virus at 1 nl/s using a Syringe Pump (KD Scientific, Holliston, MA). Volume of injected virus was 300 nl, injected in 2 150 nl increments at 2 different depths: 500 and 250 µm beneath the brain surface for V1 (targeting layers 2/3 and 5), and 700 and 800 µm for the PFC. The syringe was left in place for 5-10 minutes after the injection to allow the virus solution to diffuse and then very slowly raised to the surface to prevent the backflow. Muscimol (TMR-X conjugate; HelloBio, Princeton, NJ) was injected in the same manner, volume and at the same PFC coordinates of trained term mice at 1.6 mM concentration.

Headplates were attached after the Scotchbond adhesive application for animals that received no virus injection, or immediately after the virus injection for those that did. The headplate (stainless steel, SendCutSend, Reno, NV) was attached with dental cement (RelyX Ultimate, 3M). After the cement was cured, the well of the headplate was filled with silicone elastomer (Reynold Advanced Materials, Brighton, MA) to protect the skull.

If the mice received Rimadyl for analgesia, they were given Rimadyl dissolved in hydrogel (1% food-grade agar in distilled water) during the recovery. Animals were group-housed after the implantation and monitored daily for signs of shock or infection. On the day of electrophysiological recording, the animals were anesthetized as above and craniotomies (~0.5 mm in diameter) were made above V1, PFC and cerebellum with 18G needles. If mice were injected with viruses, the existing craniotomies were reopened. The brain surface was covered in 2-3% low melting point agarose (Promega, Madison, WI) in sterile saline and then capped with silicone elastomer. Animals were allowed to recover for 1.5-2 h before the recording.

Electrophysiology and optogenetics
For the recording sessions, mice were placed in the head-plate holder above an aluminum mesh treadmill and allowed to habituate for 5-10 minutes. The silicone plug was removed, the reference (insulated silver wire electrode; A-M Systems, Carlsborg, WA) was placed in cerebellum and the well was covered with warm sterile saline. A multisite electrode spanning all cortical layers (A1x16-5mm-50-177-A16; Neuronexus Technologies, Ann Arbor, MI) was coated with DiI (Invitrogen) to allow post hoc insertion site verification and then inserted in the V1 through the craniotomy. For PFC, a 4x4 shank probe (A4x4-3mm-50-125-177-A16) was used for the recordings, coated with DiI, DiO or DiD based on the type of fluorophore used in the experiment (mCherry or EGFP; listed in Viruses). The electrodes were slowly (5-10 µm/s) lowered to the appropriate depth: 800 µm for the PFC and until the uppermost recording site had entered the brain for the V1 and allowed to settle for 15-30 minutes. For optogenetics, a 473 nm laser diode with 0.4 µm fiber tip (0.22 NA, Doric Lenses, Quebec, Canada) was lowered to the craniotomy. 10 ms square pulses were delivered at 3-5 mW/mm2 (200 pulses at 0.5 Hz) using Spike2 (CED, Cambridge, UK) after the last recording session for optogenetic identification of neuronal subtypes (optotagging). The well was filled with 3% agarose prior to the recordings to stabilize the electrode and the whole region was kept moist with surgical gelfoam soaked in sterile saline (Pfizer, MA). The signals from the recording probes were fed into a 16-channel amplifier (Model 3500; A-M Systems, Sequim, WA) and amplified 200x, before being sampled at 25 kHz using Spike2 and Power 1401-3 data acquisition unit (CED). After the recording ended, the electrodes were slowly retracted, and the well was cleaned and protected with silicone elastomer.

Visual stimuli
For visual stimuli, blank screen was generated with MATLAB (MathWorks, Natick, MA) using the PsychToolBox extension (Brainard, 1997) and presented on a gamma corrected 27” LCD. The screen was centered 20-25 cm from the mouse’s right eye, covering ~80° of visual space. For calculating baseline orientation selectivity, sinusoidal gratings at 6 orientations 30° apart were presented at 100% contrast at 0.15 cpd, with 1 s long stimuli and 1 s interstimulus interval (blank screen). For visual discrimination training, visual stimuli (120° and 60° gratings) were presented at 0.15 cpd and 100% contrast in a random sequence for 3 seconds, followed by a 15 second long interstimulus interval (blank screen). Presentation of 120° triggered the delivery of 10µl of water through a syringe pump (New Era Pump Systems, Farmingdale, NY), while the presentation of 60° had no consequence.

Behavior
4-7 days after the headpost implantation, mice were gradually water-restricted (from 3 ml of water/day to 1 ml of water/day) for 5-7 days. Food was available ad libitum. Mice were weighed daily and their weight was maintained at 85% of initial weight to prevent dehydration. During water restriction, mice were gradually habituated to handling by the experimenters, the treadmill, and the water delivery spout during daily habituation sessions. After water restriction, the visual discrimination training began, where mice were head fixed above the treadmill and a stainless-steel gavage needle (18G) was positioned near the mouse’s mouth for water delivery. The pump was controlled by the Power 1401-3 data acquisition interface (CED) for lick detection. Mice were trained in 2 daily sessions consisting of 50 120° and 60° presentations each, for a total of 200 trials per day. Licks of the spout during the 10 s after the onset of stimulus presentation were quantified according to the signal detection theory as Hits (the fraction of trials in which the mouse licked to the 120° orientation), Misses (the fraction of trials in which the mouse failed to lick to the 120° orientation), False Alarms (the fraction of trials in which the mouse licked to the 60° orientation) and Correct Rejections (the fraction of trials in which the mouse failed to lick to the 60° orientation), where the performance was measured as discriminability (d’) = z(H)-z(FA). Mice were trained until they achieved a d’ of 2 or above for 3 consecutive sessions or up to 4000 trials if they failed to reach the criterion.

For open field, mice were placed in a 24x24 inch plexiglass arena after a brief habituation to the room and the experimenters. Their activity was recorded for 10 minutes and analyzed using an open-source toolbox.

For measuring locomotor behavior during task performance, a small piezoelectric disc was placed in contact with the treadmill and the signal was digitized using Power 1401-3 and Spike2. Waveform averages in response to both cues were constructed using Spike2 and used to compare the amount of treadmill movement during the training.

Animals were monitored for signs of distress for the duration of the experiment. Animals that developed corneal damage, cataracts, and symptoms that had the potential to impact their behavior or physiology (such as immobility and other signs of pain, sudden weight loss or impeded weight gain) were excluded from the study. All mice except those in the MFP Term and Environmental Enrichment groups underwent electrophysiology either at the beginning or at the end of the training, or both. If the animals were recorded at the onset of training, that was counted as the first training session.

Histology and imaging
After the last training session or electrophysiological recording, mice were anesthetized with a mixture of ketamine and xylazine and transcardially perfused with warm 0.1M phosphate buffer, followed by warm 4% paraformaldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences, Hatfield, PA). Brains were postfixed 1 hr at room temperature, followed by overnight fixation at 4°C. Brains were sectioned into 40-80 µm sections using a vibratome and stored in 1x phosphate buffered saline (PBS) and 0.01% sodium azide. For immunohistochemistry, sections were rinsed in PBS, non-specific binding was blocked with 3% normal horse serum (heat inactivated, ThermoFisher, Waltham, MA) and 0.3% Triton-X100 (Sigma-Aldrich) in PBS (sterile filtered). Antibodies were incubated overnight at 4°C. Parvalbumin (anti-goat) was used at 1/200 (Swant, Belinzona, Switzerland) and detected with donkey anti-goat Alexa647 (ThermoFisher). After staining, sections were rinsed in distilled water, mounted on glass slides, briefly dried, and coverslipped with Aquamount (Polysciences, Warrington, PA). Images were acquired using Leica Stellaris 8 at 2048x2048 resolution using 10x HC PLAN FLUOTAR air (NA=0.3 for tiling) or 40x HC PL APO CS2 (NA=1.3) oil immersion objective.

Electrophysiological and behavioral data analysis
Locomotion measured with piezoelectric sensors was analyzed in Spike2 (CED) using waveform averaging and cues as triggers. Spikes were isolated from the recordings using template matching in Spike2 (CED). Briefly, the recordings were band-pass filtered (0.7-7 kHz) and smoothed (0.1 ms). Threshold for detection was set at 3 SDs of the mean baseline (blank screen) and a window of 0.9-1 ms. Isolated units were clustered using waveform properties (amplitude, spike half-width and slope of repolarization), and the clusters were checked manually for quality in addition to confirming there were no spikes during the refractory period (2 ms) using interval histograms. Units with refractory period violations or units with large variations in amplitude (>10%) were excluded from analysis. For orientation selectivity, custom-written scripts in Spike2 were used to plot the baseline-subtracted responses of isolated units to the presented orientations (10 ms bin) and construct a tuning curve, which was then fitted with a Gaussian to determine the preferred (Opref) and orthogonal (Oorth) orientations, and calculate the orientation selectivity index (OSI) as (Rpref - Rorth)/(Rpref + Rorth), where R is the firing rate at preferred and orthogonal orientations. We considered the neurons with at least 3x elevated firing rate to the preferred orientation (averaged over 0.8 s and compared to averaged 0.2 s of baseline) as visually responsive. Tuning width was calculated as half-width at half-maximum of the Opref.

For optotagging, spikes were isolated from optogenetic recording sessions and PSTHs (0.1-1 ms bin) were constructed in response to the laser pulses. Units with reliable responses (>50%) of trials and short latencies (within 10 ms of the laser pulse) were considered optotagged and their waveforms were used to identify their spiking during the task performance. Unit waveforms were further compared between optotagging and task recordings for quality assurance. Units whose waveforms differed by more than 10% in amplitude and width between the two sessions were discarded from analysis.

Selectivity indices (SIs) were calculated from 10 ms peristimulus time histogram (PSTHs) as (Rcue - Rbaseline)/(Rcue + Rbaseline), where Rcue is the firing rate during the initial 1-1.5 s presentation of 120° and 60° stimuli. Behavioral responses during the task were analyzed using custom scripts in Spike2 by converting the detected licks into events and constructing PSTHs in response to the non-rewarded cue during the 2 possible outcomes (Correct Rejection and False Alarm).

Stationary and moving stages were not analyzed separately as animals were typically walking in short bouts during the recordings. Recordings where large motion artifacts were present when the animal was simply balancing on the treadmill or grooming were excluded from analysis, along with recordings from locations outside of the PFC or V1 (as determined through post-hoc mapping of insertion sites).

Quantification and statistical analysis
All analyses were performed with the researchers blind to the condition. Statistical analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism 9.0 (GraphPad Inc., La Jolla, USA), R and JASP, as indicated in text and figure legends. N refers to the number of animals or single units, as indicated in figure legends or in text. For orientation selectivity analysis, OSIs, proportions of selective cells (OSI>0.3) and tuning width (OSI>0.3) means (normal data distribution, Shapiro-Wilk test) or medians (non-normal distribution) were calculated per mouse before comparison. For comparison of preferred orientations, selective neurons (OSI>0.3) were only segregated by group (Term/Preterm). For all other analyses, units significantly modulated by cues were determined through comparison of pre-cue and post-cue firing using Wilcoxon signed rank test. The proportions of significantly modulated units (positively and negatively) were determined and reported per animal, and PSTHs and SIs represent significantly modulated units. PSTHs were compared using permutation test of area under the curve (AUC) calculated from 0.5 s precue and 1 s (V1) or 3 s (PFC) postcue activity (10 ms bins). Cue representation was determined as (%R-%NR)/(%R+%NR), where %R and %NR are the proportion of significantly positively modulated units by the rewarded and non-rewarded cue, respectively. All unit data was tested for normality using Shapiro-Wilk test and data violating the assumption of normality was tested using non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney t-test, Kolmogorov-Smirnoff for comparison of distributions or non-parametric ANOVA). Normally distributed data was tested using t-tests and ANOVA with post-hoc tests for comparing groups as indicated in text and figure legends. Levene’s test was used to test homoscedasticity with appropriate corrections used for heteroscedasticity. For linear mixed model (LMM) in Fig. 2e, an LMM with Animal Group as a fixed effect and Subject and Training Day as random effects was fitted to the data using the following formula and maximum likelihood method: d’ ~ Group + (1 + Group || Subject)+(1 + Group || Training Day). To test the sex effects, LMM with Sex and Animal Group as fixed effects and Subject and Training Day as random effects was fitted using the following formula and maximum likelihood method: d’ ~ Sex + Animal Group+ (1+ Sex + Animal Group | Subject)+(1+Sex+AnimalGroup|TrainingDay). For Fig. 2i, lick counts were averaged per 20 trials and an LMM with Animal Group and Trial Block as fixed effects and Subject as the random effect was fitted to the data using the following formula and maximum likelihood method: Lick count ~ Group + Trial block + (1 + Group + Trial Block | Animal). For Fig. 6b, an LMM with Age as a fixed effect and Subject and Training Day was fitted to the data using the following formula and maximum likelihood method: d’ ~ Age + (1 + Age | Training Day)+(1 + Age | Animal). For Fig. 7b, an LMM with Enrichment and Birth as fixed effects and Subject and Training Day as the random effects was fitted to the data using the following formula and maximum likelihood method: d’ ~ Enrichment + Birth + (1 + Enrichment + Birth | Subject)+(1 + Enrichment + Birth | Training Day). For linear regression, SI values from all neurons per animal were averaged and used as predictors of d’ as described in text and figure legends. For logistic regression, trial-by-trial spike timestamps were used to calculate the evoked rate per trial (number of spikes in a 3 s window post cue - number of spikes in a 3 s window pre cue). As behavioral outcomes were biased towards Correct Rejection, random oversampling was used to balance the datasets. Data are reported as mean ± SEM (standard error of mean) or median ± MAD (median absolute deviation), as indicated in text or figure legends, where N represents the number of animals or the number of single units. Target power for all sample sizes was 0.8 and alpha was set to 0.05.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this study, McCoy et al present a significant set of findings documenting the electrophysiological and behavioral consequences of preterm birth in a mouse model. Specifically they find that mice induced to be born 1 day preterm have behavioral inhibition to a go/no-go visual task as adults. This is accompanied by increased firing rates in V1 and ACC and increased firing to go-cue but reduced modulation in ACC to the no-go cue. These results are compared to other data showing similar results in adolescent mice to suggest pre-term mice maintain a persistent ‘adolescent’ mode of processing that is impairing their task performance. This is an important set of physiological findings that leads to an interesting conceptual conclusion. This work is an important advance in our understanding of the circuit and cognitive basis of neural issues linked to preterm birth. Overall the manuscript is very well written, the studies are properly designed, appropriately powered (within the limitations of mouse ephys), and appropriately analyzed.
I do believe there is one major sticking point that needs to be addressed before this work can be published, as well as a number of major improvements that should be considered to increase the impact of the work.
Critical point: Firing rates for ostensible single units throughout the study are nearly an order of magnitude higher than other published studies. The resting rates are similar to visually evoked rates observed by multiple other labs. This undermines confidence in the results, which are likely multi-units or severely biased to very high firing rate sub-populations. This discrepancy needs to resolved and integrated into the interpretation of the results.
Major points:
(1) Unless I am mistaken, the correlation of preterm behavior and ephys with ‘adolescent’ coding is based on a single pre-print, which used calcium imaging to an auditory cue. While the similarities are indeed pretty striking, the absence of relevant adolescent data in this paper and the fact that the reference remains a preprint at this point suggests that the title should be changed to better reflect actual behavioral and physiological differences, rather than the larger implication. The authors are strongly encouraged to pursue this correspondence in their discussion of course.
(2) There is no discussion of the potential depth of the units recorded. It is not required they break the recordings down by depth and layer, but reporting where the majority of units were located is important.
(3) Percentage of visually responsive units in V1 and firing rate increases to preferred orientation should be presented.
(4) Why no separation of FS and RS neurons in V1 as for AAC? If there is no compelling reason these should be separated and analyzed as for AAC.
(5) Why does the analysis switch to z-score normalized firing rates in figure 5? For comparison with previous data absolute firing rates should be used, unless there is a compelling reason.
(6) lines 241-242 Firing rates are rarely normally distributed, but more likely to be log-normal. Normal descriptive statistics (mean/SEM) are likely inappropriate so should use log transformed or non-normal appropriate (median, percentiles).
Minor
Were all animals recorded included in the analysis, or were some excluded for technical reasons?
236 and Fig 1: 6 Orientations or 12?
272 “‘errors of omission” is this the same as “Miss”?
Fig 3 Define R and NR, preferably on graph or at least clearly in Legend.

### Reviewer 3

In this study, the authors investigate how preterm birth affects cognitive function and visual information processing by recording neural activity in the V1 and ACC of mice during a Go/No-go task using electrophysiological techniques. They demonstrate that preterm mice exhibit a higher FA rate in the Go/No-go task, despite showing comparable orientation selectivity in V1 neurons to term controls. Furthermore, they show that both V1 and ACC neurons in preterm mice respond differently to visual stimuli during the task. Using optogenetic tagging, they also identify abnormalities in the visual processing of V1-projecting ACC neurons and ACC-FS neurons. The authors conducted experiments using both male and female mice, employed appropriate control groups, and used suitable methods and analyses to address the important question of how preterm birth impacts cognitive function. However, as described more in detail below, there are significant limitations to the interpretation of the data. Notably, the study lacks an investigation of causality, which diminishes its impact.
Major comments:
1) The study does not provide any causal link between neural activity changes of studied circuit (V1 projecting ACC neurons or FS-ACC neurons) and behavioral changes (increased FA) in pre-term mice. A key hypothesis in this manuscript is that overactivation of ACC-FS neurons leads to decreased activity of V1-projecting ACC neurons, resulting in reduced V1 activity in No-go trial and an increased FA rate. However, none of these causal relationships have been demonstrated, leaving the study less mechanistic. Without a demonstration of direct manipulations of neural circuits during behavior impacting behavior, observed neural changes may not be related to behavioral changes, leaving the study descriptive.
2) It is unclear if the observed neural and behavioral deficits in preterm mice reflect deficits in learning or/and discrimination. Throughout the manuscript, these two concepts are not clearly considered separately. Due to the trajectory difference (especially FA) during training phase, it is highly likely that there is a deficit in learning. Demonstration of neural correlate of learning trajectory would be informative to enhance the mechanistic significance of this study (especially if the study does not provide causal link between circuit activity and behavior).
3) Given that V1 activity is known to be enhanced by locomotion, extent and timing of locomotion on the treadmill during the task should be analyzed to rule out that neural changes are not confounded by locomotion.
4) Preterm mice show a lower Hit rate even in the naïve state (Fig 2G). This raises questions about potential motivational deficits, which can be assessed by different tasks such as progressive ratio test.
5) While the activity of FS and RS neurons is analyzed separately in Fig 4, the activity of V1 neurons in Fig 3 is not divided into these categories. It is unclear why FS and RS neurons were not differentiated for V1 activity, particularly as the distinction between excitatory and inhibitory neurons in V1 could provide critical insights into the observed changes.
6) Inclusion of “Adolescent-like” in the title misleading. While author cited relevant literatures, they did not examine the neural activity nor behavior using the same task used in this study. Authors should consider conducting experiments in adolescent mice to support the claim, or “Adolescent-like” should be removed from the title, result section, and limited to the discussion section.
Other comments:
-In Fig 2C, the Miss marker (water droplet) is present, but the cross marker is missing.
-How were trained mice defined in Fig 2G? Were only animals that passed the criteria included, or were all animals analyzed at their final session? If the latter, it would be important to compare only those that passed the criteria to see whether FA rate differences remain.
-In Fig 3G, V1 activity during FA trials does not appear to increase significantly in the Term group. The sustained activity in V1 shown in Fig 3C should be further discussed regarding whether it genuinely reflects premotor activity.
-The authors claim that elevated firing rates in preterm mice are unlikely due to licking during the task (L312), but Supplementary Fig S3 shows that Preterm mice have significantly more licks per trial than Term mice. Without investigating the correlation between lick count and sustained activity, this conclusion is premature. Correlating lick count with sustained activity and demonstrating a lack of correlation would strengthen this argument.
-Fig 3D shows a distribution of MI values where some V1 neurons exhibit higher MI and others lower MI in Preterm mice. It is unclear whether the average MI for V1 neurons in Preterm mice is genuinely higher than for neurons in Term mice. Showing vertical lines indicating group means would clarify this point.
-Are the data in Fig 4E limited to RS neurons? Clearly separating RS and FS neurons and presenting the data would improve clarity.
-Figure 4K is missing.
-The statement on L427 ("stronger positive modulation by the rewarded cue despite no change in the firing rates") is confusing. Since MI is calculated using firing rates, the claim of "no change in firing rates" is misleading. While statistical significance may not have been detected, differences are evident in the traces.
-The claim in L443 that deficits are "not as severe as in the V1" (Fig 3) is unclear. Based on the MI values, changes in V1-projecting ACC neurons appear larger. Moreover, throughout the manuscript, the overlap between the bars of MI histograms for each group makes it difficult to interpret the data. Adjusting the colors or the presentation style of the graphs could improve readability.
-The degree of overlap between opto-tagged FS neuron data in Fig 6 and FS neuron data classified by spike width in Fig 4 should be presented in the supplementary figure. If discrepancies exist, these should be discussed.
-In Fig 7B, the authors claim that environmental enrichment (ENR) accelerates learning in the Term group compared to the standardly housed (STD) condition. However, the initial performance on Day 0 appears worse, and there seems to be no difference in final performance or days to reach criterion.
-Since both male and female data were collected, the authors should explicitly show whether there were any sex differences in the supplementary figures.

## Authors' Response to Round 1

POINT-BY-POINT RESPONSE TO REVIEWS
Introduction and response to general concerns
We greatly appreciate the Reviewers’ support, critiques and suggestions, and we think they
significantly improved the manuscript and the quality of our analyses. Before we address the
concerns point by point below, we would like to highlight major revisions to our study. Major
textual revisions are highlighted in light grey throughout the revised manuscript.
1. We consulted Dr. Xin Cynthia Tong, a mathematician in our Department, who is an
expert in quantitative approaches. She helped reanalyze all our data, which we hope
addressed concerns about data analysis. New analysis approaches made some of the
differences between experimental groups even more pronounced, especially in the cue-
evoked firing and the distribution of selectivity indices. While our findings remain the
same, i.e. the representation and processing of task cues in preterm mice is altered
compared to term mice, some of our conclusions are revised considering the new
analyses.
2. Revised analysis revealed that the N of units significantly responsive to the non-
rewarded cue when split by behavioral outcomes for optotagging experiments was too
low to comfortably draw conclusions. We therefore focused the results derived from
optotagged neurons solely on general cue representation, and we moved that data to
the supplementary material. Of note is that the data for fast-spiking neurons isolated
through bulk electrophysiology and the data for optogenetically identified fast-spiking
neurons overlaps to a large degree (new Figure 4 and Supplementary Figures 9 and 10).
3. We separated the data for the visual cortex neurons into regular and fast-spiking
neurons and to our surprise found that both neuronal populations exhibit similar task-
related hyperactivity. We revised our discussion to incorporate these new findings,
especially since the prefrontal cortex shows a different pattern of activity in RS and FS
neurons during the task.
4. To give more credence to our previous suggestion that preterm PFC resembles
adolescent PFC, we trained adolescent term mice in our task, recorded their prefrontal
activity and compared the cue representation to that of preterm mice (new Figure 6 and
Supplementary Figure 11). While our results haven’t fully recapitulated the Nieves and
Liston preprint we cite in the original submission (likely due to methodology differences),
we did find remarkable similarities between adolescents and adult term mice in the
representation and processing of the non-rewarded cue. We discuss these in the revised
manuscript, and we think that the adolescent data will be a valuable resource to the field.
5. In the original manuscript, we use the term “Modulation Index” to determine the degree
of responsivity of neurons to task cues. We revised this term to “Selectivity Index” as our
literature search found that Modulation Index is typically used to denote firing rate
alterations by behavioral states, such as attention. To emphasize that we measure
responsiveness to the sensory cues, we chose to use Selectivity Index instead. While
this was not an issue brought up by the reviewers, it was brought up by the
neuroscience community as the submission was accessible as a preprint.

In this study, McCoy et al present a significant set of findings documenting the
electrophysiological and behavioral consequences of preterm birth in a mouse model.
Specifically they find that mice induced to be born 1 day preterm have behavioral inhibition to a
go/no-go visual task as adults. This is accompanied by increased firing rates in V1 and ACC and
increased firing to go-cue but reduced modulation in ACC to the no-go cue. These results are
compared to other data showing similar results in adolescent mice to suggest pre-term mice
maintain a persistent ‘adolescent’ mode of processing that is impairing their task performance.
This is an important set of physiological findings that leads to an interesting conceptual
conclusion. This work is an important advance in our understanding of the circuit and cognitive
basis of neural issues linked to preterm birth. Overall the manuscript is very well written, the
studies are properly designed, appropriately powered (within the limitations of mouse ephys),
and appropriately analyzed.
I do believe there is one major sticking point that needs to be addressed before this work can be
published, as well as a number of major improvements that should be considered to increase
the impact of the work.
Critical point: Firing rates for ostensible single units throughout the study are nearly an order of
magnitude higher than other published studies. The resting rates are similar to visually evoked
rates observed by multiple other labs. This undermines confidence in the results, which are
likely multi-units or severely biased to very high firing rate sub-populations. This discrepancy
needs to resolved and integrated into the interpretation of the results.
We thank the reviewer for bringing this up, as well as for their later comments which
helped us resolve this discrepancy. In the original submission, we present our firing rate data
throughout the manuscript as mean±SEM. However, and as the reviewer pointed out, the firing
rate distribution is log-normal and largely reported as median±IQ range/MAD. For example in
the V1, Durand et al. report these values: L2/3 0.58 ± 0.11, L4 3.00 ± 1.14, and L5 2.86 ± 0.65
sp/s, with an average of 1.88 ± 0.25 for spontaneous, outside of any task context, activity in the
awake V1 of adult mice (Durand et al., 2016). These values are for units unsorted by width into
fast and regular spiking (FS and RS). Please note that they did not report whether the spread of
data reported is IQR or another measure. We separated our data into Upper (putative 2/3) and
Lower (4-6) layers through analysis of visually evoked potentials (VEPs), where layer 4 has the
shortest latency VEP. and found somewhat higher values in adult term mice: Upper layers:
0.88±0.74 spikes/s, Lower layers: 4.1±3.2 spikes/s, and an average for all units at 2.41±1.01
spikes/s. We report only the last value in the manuscript and have changed our reporting
throughout to median±MAD for all lognormal data (except peristimulus time histograms). Of note
is that task training increases the overall firing rate (Maor et al., 2019) and, in our hands, placing
the animals in the task context also increases firing. We show this for the V1 in the manuscript,
but we found the same to be true for the PFC.
It is certainly possible that we captured multiunit responses in our data as spike sorting
is never perfect, and we discuss this in the revised manuscript. However, Durand et al. also
reported that mice rarely ran or walked during the recordings, which is why they did not
separate the data into stationary and moving. In our hands, habituated adult mice typically
spend a significant amount of time on the treadmill walking at different speeds, which is why we
have not separated the data into stationary and moving (see figure below). It is likely that this
somewhat elevated the firing rates in our dataset as locomotion is known to enhance them (Niell

single unit data as individual points, for example Figure 4 in (Glickfeld et al., 2013), and found

Major points:
(1) Unless I am mistaken, the correlation of preterm behavior and ephys with ‘adolescent’
coding is based on a single pre-print, which used calcium imaging to an auditory cue. While the
similarities are indeed pretty striking, the absence of relevant adolescent data in this paper and
the fact that the reference remains a preprint at this point suggests that the title should be
changed to better reflect actual behavioral and physiological differences, rather than the larger
implication. The authors are strongly encouraged to pursue this correspondence in their
discussion of course.
The reviewer is correct-the study we cite remains a preprint, and it used a different
methodology. We, however, decided to pursue this issue experimentally as we were
unsuccessful in our attempts to identify the circuit(s) that drive the impairments in preterm mice
(please see our response to Reviewer 3). We were able to confirm some similarities between
adolescent and adult preterm PFC: they both have a weak representation of the non-rewarded
cue in RS neurons, the peristimulus time histograms (PSTHs) of their prefrontal FS neurons
during the task are very similar, and their evoked responses to the non-rewarded cue classify
the behavioral outcomes to that cue at a similar accuracy (Figures 6 and Supplementary Figure
9). Given the differences in the processing of the rewarded cue, having “adolescent-like” in the
title was not justified and we have replaced it with what we think is the main finding of our study,
as the reviewer suggested.
Some of our findings are different from the Nieves and Liston, 2023, but we think that is due to
methodology used. As the reviewer mentioned, Nieves and Liston used 2-photon imaging after
an auditory task, while we used electrophysiology in a visual task. These two approaches, while
complementary, detect different cell populations. Despite this, we were able to confirm their
main finding, i.e. that the overall activity in adolescent PFC is shifted towards the rewarded cue
at the expense of the non-rewarded one.
(2) There is no discussion of the potential depth of the units recorded. It is not required they
break the recordings down by depth and layer, but reporting where the majority of units were
located is important.
This is an important point-we now state that the neurons in the V1 are recorded from all layers.
For the PFC, most of our recordings were from deeper portion of layer 2/3 going to layer 6 as
we tried to avoid recording close to the midline (see minor points response). We revised Figure
4 to include an image of the electrode tracks.
(3) Percentage of visually responsive units in V1 and firing rate increases to preferred
orientation should be presented.
The percentage of units that are considered selective for oriented gratings is presented in
Figure 1d and this is what we define as visually-responsive for this study. We clarify this now in
the methods section in the revised manuscript (lines 218-220), and we also report the firing rate
increase to the preferred orientation (over baseline, line 309-312). We find that our values are
similar to what other studies report [such as (Wang et al., 2010), which also reports the fraction
of neurons with OSI>0.3].
(4) Why no separation of FS and RS neurons in V1 as for AAC? If there is no compelling reason
these should be separated and analyzed as for AAC.
We include the separation of V1 neurons into FS and RS in the revised manuscript (new Figure
3) and we would like to thank the reviewers for bringing this up-indeed, there was no reason to
omit it in the first place, and we apologize for this lapse. We found that both RS and FS neurons
in preterm V1 have elevated firing during the task. While surprising, as we expected weakened
inhibition like in the PFC, this is in line with the powerful top-down modulation of the V1 during
task performance.
(5) Why does the analysis switch to z-score normalized firing rates in figure 5? For comparison
with previous data absolute firing rates should be used, unless there is a compelling reason.
We present all data now as raw firing rates. While PSTHs are the only instance where the firing
rates are presented as mean±SEM, we changed the scale to logarithmic to indicate that the
data is not normally distributed.
(6) lines 241-242 Firing rates are rarely normally distributed, but more likely to be log-normal.
Normal descriptive statistics (mean/SEM) are likely inappropriate so should use log transformed
or non-normal appropriate (median, percentiles).
As suggested, we changed all our reporting of log-normally distributed data to median±MAD
and indicate in the Methods that all data was first tested for normality before conducting other

Reviewer #2
The manuscript by McCoy and colleagues investigates the representation and processing of
behaviorally salient sensory stimuli in the V1 and PFC of adult preterm-born mice. Combining
behavioral assessment with in vivo electrophysiology, it shows that preterm birth causes major
deficits, especially in the function of prefrontal circuits for error monitoring. The topic is timely
and the main conclusions, as they are currently listed, of high relevance. I found particularly
interesting the limited role of environmental enrichment on the prematurity-induced cognitive
dysfunction. The complex experimental design and technically-demanding methodologies are
well chosen to address the key questions. However, my overall enthusiasm for the manuscript is
dampened by the wealth of imperfections, errors and especially, by the poor analyses and
statistics. The last is critical, since the conclusions of the study rely on correct analytical tools.
The manuscript requires a comprehensive revision of the analyses and, if necessary, correction
of the conclusions, before pursuing with the review.
We appreciate the concerns brought up and we have completely revised our analysis for the
resubmission. We consulted with a colleague who is a mathematician and an expert statistician
(Dr. Xin Cynthia Tong), who helped us reanalyze all the data. We would like to add that she
brought up the same concerns after reading the first version of the manuscript. While our main
findings after reanalysis did not change, some of the conclusions did, as the reviewer (correctly)
implied.

We added a line immediately after that sentence (line 226-228) to clarify that a change in unit
amplitude of 10% or more between the two recording sessions warranted the exclusion of that
unit from analyses as such high amplitude variability indicates either unit/probe drift or multiunit
contamination.

does not appear in the formula that is given. Also: paired t-test seems like an inappropriate test

Rvar was a copy/paste error and we apologize. This is corrected in the revised version of the
manuscript. In the revised version, we reanalyzed our unit data with tests appropriate for log-
normally distributed data. For determining significant cue modulation, Wilcoxon paired signed
rank test was used, for comparison of firing rates Mann Whitney test was used, and we used K-
S test to compare distributions (all of these and others are indicated in the methods and
appropriate sections throughout the manuscript). Instead of t-tests of AUCs, we use the
permutation test of PSTH AUCs in the revised version of the manuscript. While our results
remained largely the same, the significance is different with the new analysis.
Lines 232-233: could the authors speculate as to what a day of prematurity in mice corresponds
in human pregnancies?
We briefly discuss this in the revised manuscript (line 865-872), but we must admit that this
comparison remains a challenge and a contentious issue in the field. Most studies consider
mice during the first week to 10 days of life an equivalent of a third trimester fetus, some of
which is based on electrophysiological comparison of rodent and human developing cortices
(Colonnese et al., 2010). Our unpublished data indicates that in terms of electrophysiological
activity, mice and humans share a similar developmental trajectory from birth through the first 2
weeks and one year of life, respectively, and that birth itself plays a role in patterning the
perinatal intrinsic activity in mice (which is the line of research that led us to test the long term
consequences of advancing the birth timing). Current models of prematurity-related brain injury
(term mice subjected to hypoxia and/or ischemia) do not capture the actual prematurity that, at
least according to our findings, itself has an impact on brain development. It will be important to
compare the prefrontal function in term mice subjected to hypoxia/ischemia to those in the
current study and relate both to findings in humans.

Reviewer #3
In this study, the authors investigate how preterm birth affects cognitive function and visual
information processing by recording neural activity in the V1 and ACC of mice during a Go/No-
go task using electrophysiological techniques. They demonstrate that preterm mice exhibit a
higher FA rate in the Go/No-go task, despite showing comparable orientation selectivity in V1
neurons to term controls. Furthermore, they show that both V1 and ACC neurons in preterm
mice respond differently to visual stimuli during the task. Using optogenetic tagging, they also
identify abnormalities in the visual processing of V1-projecting ACC neurons and ACC-FS
neurons. The authors conducted experiments using both male and female mice, employed
appropriate control groups, and used suitable methods and analyses to address the important
question of how preterm birth impacts cognitive function. However, as described more in detail
below, there are significant limitations to the interpretation of the data. Notably, the study lacks
an investigation of causality, which diminishes its impact.
Major comments:
1) The study does not provide any causal link between neural activity changes of studied circuit
(V1 projecting ACC neurons or FS-ACC neurons) and behavioral changes (increased FA) in
pre-term mice. A key hypothesis in this manuscript is that overactivation of ACC-FS neurons
leads to decreased activity of V1-projecting ACC neurons, resulting in reduced V1 activity in No-
go trial and an increased FA rate. However, none of these causal relationships have been
demonstrated, leaving the study less mechanistic. Without a demonstration of direct
manipulations of neural circuits during behavior impacting behavior, observed neural changes
may not be related to behavioral changes, leaving the study descriptive.
We agree with the reviewer and emphasize in the revised version that our study is descriptive,
and we discuss this limitation. We have attempted to test for causality in both ACC→V1 circuit
and in FS neurons with no success, some of which was due to methodological limitations, as we
outline below.
Firstly, we tried to manipulate both ACC→V1 and prefrontal FS neurons optogenetically but
found that prolonged light stimulation (2x day for 50 x 3 s duration) at levels that had a
physiological impact on neuronal firing led to neurotoxicity. Reducing the cue duration to 2
instead of 3 seconds did not mitigate this. We next attempted to suppress the activity of
ACC→V1 circuit with chemogenetics, which unexpectedly elevated V1 firing in controls (term
mice, see Figure 2a). Increasing the activity of FS neurons through chemogenetics in adult
preterm mice failed to improve their behavior in a pilot experiment (Figure 2b). We did not
include this data in the manuscript as the data from ACC→V1 activation will be a part on
another manuscript, and the pilot experiment with chemogenetic activation of interneurons did
not warrant collecting a full dataset. Further, after collecting the adolescent data (new Figure 6),
we now think that there is a developmental window during which these manipulations might
have more of an effect. We also mention this in our response to Reviewer 2, but our preliminary
data indicates that the alterations in the firing of prefrontal neurons in preterm mice begin at
birth, further indicating that there is a defined window for interventions after preterm birth. We
are actively addressing this issue in another study as it is beyond the scope of this manuscript.
To increase the significance of our findings and to try to shed more light on the developmental
impact of preterm birth on the PFC, we added data describing cue processing in adolescent
mice and compared it to preterm mice. We found several similarities in the representation of the
non-rewarded cue and the activity of FS neurons, which we discuss in details in the revised
version (Figure 6, Supplementary Figure 11 and associated Results and Discussion sections).
Figure 2. a) PSTH of V1 firing after administration of CNO (2.5 mg/kg) and vehicle (DMSO) to mice 30 minutes
before the onset of training. Mice were transduced with inhibitory DREADD G1 in V1-projecting PFC neurons.
Significant firing rate increase is present with CNO administration. b) Comparison of behavioral performance
of preterm mice from Figure 2 of the manuscript and preterm mice injected with S5E2-Gq in the PFC (Gq in
fast-spiking interneurons) and treated with CNO (2.5 mg/kg) 30 minutes before each training session. While
this preliminary cohort includes only 5 mice, the overlap with the standard preterm group indicates no effect of
fast-spiking interneuron activation on behavior in preterm mice.
2) It is unclear if the observed neural and behavioral deficits in preterm mice reflect deficits in
learning or/and discrimination. Throughout the manuscript, these two concepts are not clearly
considered separately. Due to the trajectory difference (especially FA) during training phase, it is
highly likely that there is a deficit in learning. Demonstration of neural correlate of learning
trajectory would be informative to enhance the mechanistic significance of this study (especially
if the study does not provide causal link between circuit activity and behavior).
This is an important point-the deficit in preterm mice is a learning deficit and we clarify this in the
revised version. In the original version, we used the terms interchangeably which is incorrect
and as the reviewer pointed out, preterm mice have a learning deficit (and not discrimination).
We now added new data that indicates altered encoding of behavioral outcomes to the non-
rewarded cue in preterm and adolescent mice, as well as a finding that re responses to the
rewarded cue are predictive of performance in preterm but not term mice, further providing
support for divergent mechanisms of learning in the two groups of mice (new Figures 4, 5 and
6). We discuss these, especially in the context of behavioral inhibition.
3) Given that V1 activity is known to be enhanced by locomotion, extent and timing of
locomotion on the treadmill during the task should be analyzed to rule out that neural changes
are not confounded by locomotion.
We discuss this also in our response to Reviewer 1, where there is an example of motion during
a recording session. We added motion tracking data during behavioral sessions to the revised
manuscript (Supplementary Figure 4A of the revised manuscript). We found no significant
differences in the extent or the timing of motion between term and preterm mice during task
performance, indicating that the elevated firing rates in preterm mice have a different origin.
4) Preterm mice show a lower Hit rate even in the naïve state (Fig 2G). This raises questions
about potential motivational deficits, which can be assessed by different tasks such as
progressive ratio test.
While we were unable to add the progressive ratio test, we analyzed the lick frequencies during
the training session as a proxy for motivation (Berditchevskaia et al., 2016). We indeed found
that lick rates significantly drop during the session, but all animal groups had a similar reduction
in lick frequencies, indicating that the motivation of preterm mice during the task is comparable
to term mice. The reviewer correctly points out low lick rates in naïve preterm mice, but they
increase throughout the training and surpass those of term mice (Supplementary Figure 4C of
the revised manuscript). We, however, plan to pursue tasks that can address motivation as well
as attention better than the current one in our future studies.
5) While the activity of FS and RS neurons is analyzed separately in Fig 4, the activity of V1
neurons in Fig 3 is not divided into these categories. It is unclear why FS and RS neurons were
not differentiated for V1 activity, particularly as the distinction between excitatory and inhibitory
neurons in V1 could provide critical insights into the observed changes.
We agree and we have added this to the revised manuscript (new Figure 3). Indeed, our data
further indicates the involvement of top-down areas in observed V1 firing changes in preterm
mice, especially since both RS and FS neurons are equally affected.
6) Inclusion of “Adolescent-like” in the title misleading. While author cited relevant literatures,
they did not examine the neural activity nor behavior using the same task used in this study.
Authors should consider conducting experiments in adolescent mice to support the claim, or
“Adolescent-like” should be removed from the title, result section, and limited to the discussion
section.
This is a very important point. As the reviewer pointed out, the connections we made with
adolescent processing were based on a different study and purely speculative. For the revision,
we trained adolescent term mice in our task and recorded their prefrontal activity (new Figure 6).
We indeed found similarities in the representation and processing of the non-rewarded cue in
adolescent and preterm mice. Still, and as we mention in our response to Reviewer 1, the
differences in the processing of the rewarded cue warrant removal of “adolescent-like” from the
title and the manuscript text. Instead, we focused on describing the differences and similarities
between the two groups of mice, as well as on larger implications of our findings. We were able
to confirm some of the findings from Nieves and Liston, 2023 and we think that the adolescent
data will be a valuable addition to the field. The differences we found in our task between term
adolescent and adult mice in prefrontal activity warrant their own study, which we are currently
pursuing.
